---
title: "Beam"
---

This page describes the beam solvers of slenderpy: the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation, its bending laws and the numerical schemes that solve it. The example pages [beam static](examples/beam_static.qmd) and [beam dynamic](examples/beam_dynamic.qmd) show them at work.

We have the following notations:

* $EI$: the bending stiffness of the beam, if it is constant along the beam. $E$ is the Young modulus and $I$ the second moment of area.
* $EI_{max}$: the maximum bending stiffness of the beam (when the bending stiffness is not constant along the beam).
* $EI_{min}$: the minimum bending stiffness of the beam (when the bending stiffness is not constant along the beam).
* $M$: the bending moment.
* $H$: the tension.
* $F$: the external forces per unit length applied on the beam.
* $m$: the mass per unit length of the beam.
* $\chi(y)$: the curvature of the beam which is a function of the displacement $y$.
* $\chi_0$: the critical curvature below which the bending moment is close to $EI_{max}$ and above which it is close to $EI_{min}$.
* $\omega_0$: the natural pulsation of the beam ($= 2 \pi f_0$ with $f_0$ the natural frequency of the beam).
* $\zeta$: the damping ratio of the beam (if equal to 1: critical damping, if less than 1: underdamped, if greater than 1: overdamped).
* $\eta$ : the hysteresis variable.

The unknown of the problem is the vertical displacement of the beam $y(x,t)$ where $x$ is the position along the beam and $t$ the time.

The exact formula for the curvature $\chi$ is:

$$
\chi_{exact}(y) = \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x ^2 } \frac{1}{\left(1 + \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}^2 \right)^{3/2}}
$$

By making a Taylor expansion at order 1 of this formula, under the assumption of small displacements, we get the following approximation for the curvature:

$$
\chi_{approx}(y) = \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x ^2 }
$$


The beam solvers are functions of a [](`~slenderpy.components.Conductor`)
and a [](`~slenderpy.components.Span`), whose ``boundary_conditions``
must be set. Two choices are made independently, by arguments:

* the bending law ([](`~slenderpy.beam.bending`)): ``model="constant"``
  for a constant bending stiffness $EI$ (``conductor.ei_max`` by default,
  or the ``ei`` argument), or ``model="varying"`` for a stiffness that falls
  from $EI_{max}$ to $EI_{min}$ with hysteresis, after the Bouc-Wen
  model, with $\chi_0$ = ``conductor.beta_flexion * span.tension``;
* the curvature ([](`~slenderpy.beam.curvature`)):
  ``approx_curvature=True`` for $\chi_{approx}$, ``False`` for
  $\chi_{exact}$.

The displacement $y$ is the vertical position of the beam, stored as
``z`` in the results (see the output contract of
[](`~slenderpy.simulation`)).

## Static

[](`~slenderpy.beam.static.shape.solve`) returns the displacement at the
nodes under a nodal load $F(x)$.

### Constant model

The equation solved in the static case is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial^2 M(y)}{\partial x ^2 } - H \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x ^2 } = F(x) \\
&M(y) = EI \chi(y)
\end{aligned}
$$


### Varying model

The equation solved in the static case is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial^2 M(y)}{\partial x ^2 } - H \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x ^2 } = F(x) \\
&M(y) = (EI_{max} \bar{\chi} + EI_{min} |\chi(y)|)(1 - \exp(- \frac{|\chi(y)|}{\bar{\chi}})) \mathrm{sign}(\chi(y)) \\
&\bar{\chi} = (1 - \frac{EI_{min}}{EI_{max}}) \chi_0
\end{aligned}
$$


### Resolution

The space derivatives are discretized with centered finite differences, on
the span nodes and a ghost node beyond each support that carries the boundary
conditions (see [Boundary Conditions](#boundary-conditions)). The
nonlinear system is solved with a damped Newton iteration, starting from the
constant-stiffness linear solution. The Jacobian is assembled analytically from
the tangent of the bending law and the Jacobian of the curvature; each step is
relaxed until it decreases the residual norm. A solve that does not converge
returns ``nan``.

## Dynamic

[](`~slenderpy.beam.dynamic.solve_dynamic`) returns the time history of
the beam under a force ``force(x, t, y, z, vy, vz) -> (fy, fz)`` (see
[](`~slenderpy.force.core`); the beam is planar and uses ``fz``). By
default it starts at rest from the static shape under the force at the initial
time.

### Constant model

The equation solved in the dynamic case is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&m\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t ^2 } + 2m\omega_0 \zeta \frac{\partial y}{\partial t  }  + \frac{\partial^2 M}{\partial x ^2 }   - H \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x ^2 } = F(x,t) \\
&M(y) = EI \chi(y)
\end{aligned}
$$


### Varying model

The equations solved in the dynamic case are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&m\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t ^2 } + 2m\omega_0 \zeta \frac{\partial y}{\partial t  }  + \frac{\partial^2 M}{\partial x ^2 }   - H \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x ^2 } = F(x,t) \\
&M(y) = EI_{min}\chi(y) + (EI_{max} - EI_{min})\chi_0 \eta \\
& \chi_0 \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial \chi}{\partial t} - \frac{1}{2} (\frac{\partial \chi}{\partial t} |\eta| + |\frac{\partial \chi}{\partial t}| \eta)
\end{aligned}
$$


### Time discretization

Both models are integrated with the generalized-$\alpha$ scheme (Chung and
Hulbert, 1993), with the velocity $v$ and the acceleration $a$ as additional
unknowns. With $P = c v + K y + G$ the forces of the equation, the step
enforces

$$
\begin{aligned}
&m \left( (1 - \alpha_m) a^{n+1} + \alpha_m a^n \right) + (1 - \alpha_f) P^{n+1} + \alpha_f P^n = (1 - \alpha_f) F^{n+1} + \alpha_f F^n \\
&v^{n+1} = v^n + \Delta t \left( (1 - \gamma) a^n + \gamma a^{n+1} \right) \\
&y^{n+1} = y^n + \Delta t v^n + \Delta t^2 \left( (\tfrac{1}{2} - \beta) a^n + \beta a^{n+1} \right)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\gamma = \frac{1}{2} - \alpha_m + \alpha_f$ and
$\beta = \frac{(1 - \alpha_m + \alpha_f)^2}{4}$, which make the scheme second
order and, for $\alpha_m \le \alpha_f \le \frac{1}{2}$, unconditionally stable
on linear problems,
$K = EI_{lin} D_4 - H D_2$ the linear part of the equation,
$c = 2 m \omega_0 \zeta$ the damping coefficient, and
$G = D_2 M - EI_{lin} D_4 y$ the nonlinear remainder. $EI_{lin}$ is
$EI$ for the constant model and $EI_{min}$ for the varying one; the
split between $K$ and $G$ is purely algebraic. Eliminating $a^{n+1}$ and
$y^{n+1}$ leaves the velocity as the only unknown, with the matrix
$A = (1 - \alpha_m) m I_d + w c I_d + w h K$ plus the boundary rows, where
$w = \gamma \Delta t (1 - \alpha_f)$ and $h = \beta \Delta t / \gamma$ is the
derivative of $y^{n+1}$ with respect to $v^{n+1}$. The initial acceleration
comes from the equation of motion at ``t0``; at the ghost nodes it follows the
boundary relations, like the position and the velocity, so that the Newmark
updates keep the relations on the position.

#### Scheme parameters

$\alpha_m$ and $\alpha_f$ are the ``alpha_m`` and ``alpha_f`` arguments of
[](`~slenderpy.beam.dynamic.solve_dynamic`) and
[](`~slenderpy.stockbridge.coupling.beam_coupling.solve_dynamic_with_sb`).
Particular cases:

| $\alpha_m$ | $\alpha_f$ | scheme |
|------------|------------|--------|
| 0 | 0 | trapezoidal rule (Crank-Nicolson), no numerical damping |
| 0 | $-\alpha \in [0, 1/3]$ | HHT-$\alpha$ (Hilber, Hughes and Taylor, 1977) |
| $\le 0$ | 0 | WBZ-$\alpha$ (Wood, Bossak and Zienkiewicz, 1980) |
| $\frac{2 \rho_\infty - 1}{\rho_\infty + 1}$ | $\frac{\rho_\infty}{\rho_\infty + 1}$ | generalized-$\alpha$ with spectral radius $\rho_\infty$ at infinite frequency |

[](`~slenderpy.beam.dynamic.generalized_alpha`) returns the last pair, which
for a given $\rho_\infty$ damps the resolved modes the least. The defaults,
$\alpha_m = 0.1$ and $\alpha_f = 0.37$, are that pair for
$\rho_\infty \approx 0.58$, rounded.

The trapezoidal rule is second order and energy conserving, but it does not
damp the modes the time step cannot resolve: they flip sign from one step to
the next. With the varying model these oscillations switch the Bouc-Wen
branches, and the solution stops converging in time on medium spans and
jumpers. With too little damping, a saturated jumper (5 m, 50 N) in free
vibration with 1 mm of motion keeps chattering between branches at its
reversals; its solution turns chaotic and does not converge in time.

What suppresses the chattering is the damping of the modes at 2 to 10 steps
per period, not $\rho_\infty$ itself. Every scheme above damps the resolved
modes with a ratio growing as $(\omega \Delta t)^3$; at equal $\rho_\infty$,
generalized-$\alpha$ damps them four times less than HHT, but it also damps
the modes at a few steps per period less. Algorithmic damping ratio of an
undamped oscillator, from the linear analysis of the scheme:

| scheme | $\rho_\infty$ | 5 steps per period | 10 | 25 | 50 | 100 |
|--------|---------------|--------------------|----|----|----|-----|
| HHT, $\alpha = -0.2$ | 2/3 | 1.7e-2 | 3.3e-3 | 2.5e-4 | 3.2e-5 | 4.0e-6 |
| generalized-$\alpha$ | 2/3 | 5.3e-3 | 8.9e-4 | 6.2e-5 | 7.9e-6 | 9.9e-7 |
| default (0.1, 0.37) | 0.59 | 1.1e-2 | 2.0e-3 | 1.5e-4 | 1.9e-5 | 2.4e-6 |
| generalized-$\alpha$ = HHT, $\alpha = -1/3$ | 1/2 | 2.0e-2 | 3.8e-3 | 2.8e-4 | 3.6e-5 | 4.6e-6 |

The default is about the least damping that keeps the jumper converging. It
damps the resolved modes 40 % less than HHT with $\alpha = -0.2$, the scheme
the solver used before. The free decay of a single mode checks the table
(``test_resolved_mode_damping_matches_the_scheme_analysis``), within 3 %.

The time convergence test below (three spans, three loadings, varying model)
was run over the parameters to find the range that works in each case; a
case fails when the error does not fall at each refinement or falls by less
than 4 times overall:

| scheme | $\alpha_m$, $\alpha_f$ | long span | medium span | jumper |
|--------|------------------------|-----------|-------------|--------|
| trapezoidal | 0, 0 | all | free, fast | none |
| HHT $\alpha = -0.05$ | 0, 0.05 | all | all | slow, fast |
| HHT $\alpha = -0.1$ | 0, 0.1 | all | all | all (free at the limit, 4.0) |
| HHT $\alpha = -0.2$ | 0, 0.2 | all | all | all |
| generalized-$\alpha$, $\rho_\infty = 0.8$ | 0.33, 0.44 | all | all | none |
| generalized-$\alpha$, $\rho_\infty = 2/3$ | 0.2, 0.4 | all | all | slow, fast |
| generalized-$\alpha$, $\rho_\infty = 0.62$ | 0.15, 0.38 | all | all | all (free at 5.3) |
| generalized-$\alpha$, $\rho_\infty = 0.6$ | 0.125, 0.375 | all | all | all (free at 5.7) |
| default | 0.1, 0.37 | all | all | all |
| generalized-$\alpha$, $\rho_\infty = 0.5$ | 0, 0.33 | all | all | all |
| generalized-$\alpha$, $\rho_\infty = 0.3$ | -0.31, 0.23 | all | free, fast (slow at 3.7) | all |
| generalized-$\alpha$, $\rho_\infty = 0$ | -1, 0 | all | free, fast (slow at 3.8) | all |

The long span, nearly elastic, converges whatever the parameters. The jumper
needs $\rho_\infty \le 0.62$ with generalized-$\alpha$, or $\alpha \le -0.1$
with HHT: at $\rho_\infty = 2/3$ it fails in free vibration, at 0.8 under
every loading. The medium span under the slow load is the tightest case on
$\eta$ for every scheme: the trapezoidal rule fails it by chattering, the
strongest damping ($\rho_\infty \le 0.3$) only by a total drop just under 4.
Among the values tested, the range that works in every case is
$0.5 \le \rho_\infty \le 0.62$ for generalized-$\alpha$ and
$-1/3 \le \alpha \le -0.1$ for HHT, the latter at its limit. These limits
hold at 20 steps per period of the loading at the coarsest step.

#### Origin of the scheme

The Newmark updates (Newmark, 1959) with $\gamma = 1/2$, $\beta = 1/4$ and the
equation enforced at $t^{n+1}$ are the trapezoidal rule. Within that family
the only way to damp is $\gamma > 1/2$, which drops the scheme to first order
and damps the low modes as much as the high ones (Hughes, 1987, ch. 9). The
HHT-$\alpha$ scheme (Hilber, Hughes and Taylor, 1977) keeps the Newmark
updates but weights the forces between $n$ and $n+1$, and ties $\gamma$ and
$\beta$ to that weight to stay second order. Its single parameter
$\alpha \in [-1/3, 0]$ sets the spectral radius at infinite frequency,
$\rho_\infty = (1 + \alpha) / (1 - \alpha)$, from 1 down to 1/2 only. The
WBZ-$\alpha$ scheme (Wood, Bossak and Zienkiewicz, 1980) weights the inertia
instead. Generalized-$\alpha$ (Chung and Hulbert, 1993) weights both and,
for each $\rho_\infty \in [0, 1]$, picks the pair that damps the resolved modes
the least; HHT and WBZ are special cases. The behaviour of generalized-$\alpha$
on nonlinear problems, where some of its linear properties are lost, is
analysed by Erlicher, Bonaventura and Bursi (2002).

All these schemes also lengthen the period of a mode. At equal
$\rho_\infty = 2/3$, from the linear analysis, damping ratio $\bar{\xi}$ and
period elongation $\bar{T}/T - 1$:

| steps per period | HHT $\bar{\xi}$ | WBZ $\bar{\xi}$ | generalized-$\alpha$ $\bar{\xi}$ | HHT $\bar{T}/T - 1$ | generalized-$\alpha$ $\bar{T}/T - 1$ |
|------------------|-----------------|-----------------|----------------------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------------|
| 10 | 3.3e-3 | 6.7e-3 | 8.9e-4 | 4.4e-2 | 3.8e-2 |
| 25 | 2.5e-4 | 5.4e-4 | 6.2e-5 | 7.4e-3 | 6.2e-3 |
| 50 | 3.2e-5 | 7.1e-5 | 7.9e-6 | 1.9e-3 | 1.6e-3 |
| 100 | 4.0e-6 | 8.9e-6 | 9.9e-7 | 4.7e-4 | 3.9e-4 |

WBZ damps twice as much as HHT, which is why it is not used. The algorithmic
damping ratio $\bar{\xi}$ depends on $\omega \Delta t$ only: the steps per
period that matter are those of the highest mode carrying energy, not of the
first mode, and since $\zeta$ is usually zero the scheme's damping is to be
compared with the hysteretic one (see [Time convergence](#time-convergence)).
The tables of this section are computed with the following script, on an
undamped oscillator:

```python
import numpy as np


def amplification(am, af, gamma, beta, omega_dt):
    """Damping ratio and period elongation of the generalized-alpha family
    on an undamped oscillator, state (y, v, a), dt = 1."""
    k = omega_dt**2
    lhs = np.array([[(1 - af) * k, 0.0, 1 - am], [0.0, 1.0, -gamma], [1.0, 0.0, -beta]])
    rhs = np.array([[-af * k, 0.0, -am], [0.0, 1.0, 1 - gamma], [1.0, 1.0, 0.5 - beta]])
    eig = np.linalg.eigvals(np.linalg.solve(lhs, rhs))
    lam = eig[np.argmax(np.abs(eig.imag))]
    phase = abs(np.angle(lam))
    return -np.log(abs(lam)) / phase, omega_dt / phase - 1.0


def scheme(alpha_m, alpha_f):
    gamma = 0.5 - alpha_m + alpha_f
    return alpha_m, alpha_f, gamma, 0.25 * (gamma + 0.5) ** 2


for steps in (5, 10, 25, 50, 100):
    print(steps, amplification(*scheme(0.1, 0.37), 2 * np.pi / steps))
```

#### Alternatives

Other schemes with controllable high-frequency damping and little
low-frequency damping, not implemented:

* composite schemes: the Bathe scheme (Bathe and Baig, 2005), a trapezoidal
  sub-step followed by a three-point backward difference, designed for
  nonlinear dynamics, and the $\rho_\infty$-Bathe scheme (Noh and Bathe, 2019),
  whose splitting ratio and $\rho_\infty$ are parameters. They cost two solves
  per step, two Newton loops in the nonlinear cases;
* energy-decaying and energy-momentum schemes (Kuhl and Crisfield, 1999;
  Armero and Romero, 2001), which control the energy by construction in
  nonlinear elastodynamics. They mainly address nonlinear stability, which the
  solver does not lack.

No established method was found that adapts $\alpha_m$, $\alpha_f$ during a
run from the state of the solution: the adaptive methods found adapt the time
step, with $\rho_\infty$ fixed. Two options remain untested: choosing the
parameters from $\Delta t$ and the highest frequency of interest, so that
$\bar{\xi}$ stays below a fraction of the hysteretic damping; or switching to
strong damping only near the Bouc-Wen reversals, where the chattering
starts, at the price of a local loss of order at each switch and of an energy
balance with varying weights.

For the constant model with the approximate curvature $G$ vanishes: the
problem is linear, $A$ is factorised once and each step is one solve.

In the three other cases the step is solved with a Newton iteration on its
residual, started from the velocity extrapolated from the two previous steps,
$2 v^n - v^{n-1}$, with the tangent

$$
A + w h \left( D_2 \, \mathrm{diag}\left(\frac{dM}{d\chi}\right) \frac{d\chi}{dy} - EI_{lin} D_4 \right)
$$

and a backtracking that relaxes a step increasing the residual. The hysteresis
variable is advanced fully implicitly, with the curvature increment of the
step $\Delta \chi = \chi^{n+1} - \chi^n$:

$$
\chi_0 (\eta^{n+1} - \eta^n) = \Delta \chi - \frac{1}{2} (\Delta \chi |\eta^{n+1}| + |\Delta \chi| \eta^{n+1})
$$

Since the sign of $\eta^{n+1}$ is the sign of
$\chi_0 \eta^n + \Delta \chi$, this equation has a closed-form solution,
bounded by 1 whatever the step. A fixed-point (Picard) iteration on a frozen
$A$ does not converge here: with $EI_{lin} = EI_{min}$ and a true
tangent of $EI_{max}$ its gain is $EI_{max}/EI_{min}$. A step that
does not converge stops the run; the snapshots already computed are kept and
the remaining ones are left at ``nan``.

The increment $\Delta \chi$ must be the one the curvature itself makes over
the step. Taking it as the curvature rate at the end of the step times
$\Delta t$ puts $\eta$ half a step ahead of $\chi$: in the elastic range the
hysteretic moment then leads the curvature, which acts as a numerical damping
proportional to $\Delta t$. On a 30 m span (mode 9, curvature 0.03 $\chi_0$),
that damping was 23 times the hysteretic one at 25 steps per period, and
still 2.4 times at 400 steps.

### Time convergence

The scheme is checked over three spans (ASTER 570, clamped ends), which cover
the hysteresis regimes met in practice: a long span (440 m, 39 kN), nearly
elastic; a medium span (50 m, 5 kN), around $\chi_0$; and a jumper (5 m,
50 N), whose small $\chi_0$ keeps it saturated. Each is run in free vibration,
under a point force at its first frequency and under one at 20 Hz. With 20
steps per period of the loading at the coarsest step, the error against a run
at $\Delta t / 64$ falls at each refinement to $\Delta t / 4$ and
$\Delta t / 16$, on the position, the velocity and $\eta$, by 4.6 to 240 times
overall (``test/test_beam-dynamic-convergence.py``). The order is 2 where the
hysteresis is inactive and between 1/2 and 1 where it switches, the Bouc-Wen
law not being smooth at a reversal. These runs use a Newton tolerance of
$10^{-10}$: at the default $10^{-6}$, the point where Newton stops decides on
which branch a node leaves a reversal, and the jumper run at $\Delta t / 64$
moves by up to $1.1 \cdot 10^{-7}$ m (root mean square) with the tolerance,
11 % of the error at $\Delta t / 16$.

The equivalent damping of a free decay (30 m hinged span, mode 9) is resolved
at 50 steps per period, against 23 times the hysteretic damping at 25 steps
for the former scheme (see above):

| $\chi / \chi_0$ | steps per period | damping ratio |
|-----------------|------------------|---------------|
| 0.03 | 25 | 2.7e-4 |
| 0.03 | 50 | 1.4e-4 |
| 0.03 | 100 | 1.3e-4 |
| 0.03 | 400 | 1.2e-4 |
| 1 | 25 | 2.8e-3 |
| 1 | 50 | 2.7e-3 |
| 1 | 400 | 2.7e-3 |

At $\chi / \chi_0 = 0.03$ the hysteretic damping (1.2e-4) is of the order of
the scheme's own (1.5e-4 at 25 steps per period, see above): there the step
has to resolve the mode for the decay to be the physical one. At
$\chi / \chi_0 = 1$ the scheme's damping is negligible.

### Space convergence

The same three spans and loadings are run on a coarse grid refined 2 and 4
times, against a reference refined 8 times, with the same time step on every
grid (``test/test_beam-space-convergence.py``); the static shape under gravity
is checked the same way, with both bending models. The coarse grids hold
440, 320 and 80 cells on the long span, the medium span and the jumper.

The position converges at second order once the grid resolves the bending
boundary layer $\sqrt{EI / H}$ at the clamped supports, 0.66 m on the medium
span and 6.6 m on the jumper: its error drops by 12.5 to 21 times over the
4 times refinement, against 21 for second order and 7 for first order. The
velocity and $\eta$ converge more irregularly, by 4.0 to 21 times, a grid
landing unluckily on a Bouc-Wen reversal now and then.

The 0.23 m boundary layer of the long span is not resolved by 1 m cells. Its
position still converges, by 1.9 to 3.9 times, and the static shape with the
varying model only reaches second order from about 7000 cells. The error is
small nevertheless: against a reference on 28160 cells, itself good to about
0.7 mm, the static shape (9.5 m sag) is off by 1.9 mm (root mean square at the
span eighths) at 1 m cells with the varying model and by 10 mm with the
constant one. The former one-sided slope
of the clamped supports, first order, was off by 75 mm and 62 mm.

## Energy balance

### Continuous balance

Multiplying the beam equation
$m \ddot{y} + c \dot{y} + \frac{\partial^2 M}{\partial x^2} - H \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} = F$
by the velocity $v = \dot{y}$, integrating over the span and by parts gives

$$
\frac{d}{dt} \left( E_k + E_H + E_B \right) + P_c + P_\eta + P_\chi = P_F + P_b
$$

with the kinetic, tension and bending energies

$$
E_k = \int_0^L \frac{m}{2} v^2 dx, \quad
E_H = \int_0^L \frac{H}{2} \left( \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right)^2 dx, \quad
E_B = \int_0^L \frac{EI_{lin}}{2} \chi^2 dx
$$

the powers dissipated by the damping, absorbed by the Bouc-Wen term
$M - EI_{lin} \chi = (EI_{max} - EI_{min}) \chi_0 \eta$ (varying model only)
and by the exact curvature

$$
P_c = \int_0^L c v^2 dx, \quad
P_\eta = \int_0^L (EI_{max} - EI_{min}) \chi_0 \eta \dot{\chi} dx, \quad
P_\chi = \int_0^L M \left( \frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2} - \dot{\chi} \right) dx
$$

the power of the external force $P_F = \int_0^L F v dx$ and the power of the
supports

$$
P_b = \left[ H \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} v - \frac{\partial M}{\partial x} v + M \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \right]_0^L
$$

$P_\chi$ is zero for the approximate curvature, where
$\frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2} = \dot{\chi}$. With the exact curvature
it is not: the term $\frac{\partial^2 M}{\partial x^2}$ of the equation is not
the variation of $E_B$, so part of the bending work is not stored as $E_B$.
$P_b$ is zero for fixed hinged or clamped supports.

### Usage

[](`~slenderpy.beam.dynamic.solve_dynamic`) with ``energy=True`` adds nine
scalars per output time to the results, in J:

| name | meaning |
|------|---------|
| ``kinetic_energy`` | $E_k$ |
| ``tension_energy`` | $E_H$ |
| ``bending_energy`` | $E_B$, energy stored by the linear part of the moment |
| ``external_work`` | work done by the force on the beam, gravity included |
| ``damping_work`` | energy dissipated by $\zeta$, never negative |
| ``hysteresis_work`` | work absorbed by the Bouc-Wen term, zero for the constant model |
| ``curvature_work`` | work of the moment not stored as $E_B$, zero for the approximate curvature |
| ``numerical_work`` | energy dissipated by the time scheme, mostly in the modes the step does not resolve |
| ``boundary_work`` | work provided (positive) or absorbed (negative) by the supports |

The works are cumulated from ``t0``, where they are zero, and

    kinetic_energy + tension_energy + bending_energy
        + damping_work + hysteresis_work + curvature_work + numerical_work
        - external_work - boundary_work

is constant in time.

``numerical_work`` has no continuous counterpart: it measures what the time
scheme removes, and falls quickly as the step resolves the motion. On the
440 m span below (clamped, initial shape $\sin^3$, half of whose energy lies
in the third mode, ``ns = 201``), it reaches 28 % of the initial energy after
4 periods at 20 steps per period of the first mode (under 7 for the third),
3.6 % at 50 steps and 7.6e-5 at 400 steps, with the default parameters.

### Discrete balance

The balance is computed on the discrete equation the solver solves, not with
a separate quadrature: the row $i$ of the step multiplied by
$\delta y_i = y_i^{n+1} - y_i^n$ is the work of each term over the step. The
nodes are those of the extended grid the solver works on: the span nodes and a
ghost node beyond each support (see [Boundary Conditions](#boundary-conditions)),
$N$ in all. Let $I$ be the rows the scheme solves (nodes 2 to $N-3$, the span
nodes between the supports; the others carry the boundary conditions), $J$ the
span nodes 1 to $N-2$, $\sum'_J$ a sum over $J$ weighting its end nodes, the
supports, by 1/2, $D_2$ the centered second difference,
$\bar{a} = (a^n + a^{n+1})/2$ and $\delta a = a^{n+1} - a^n$. The state
energies are

$$
E_k = \frac{m}{2} \Delta x \sum_I v_i^2, \quad
E_H = \frac{H}{2} \Delta x \sum_{j=1}^{N-3} \left( \frac{y_{j+1} - y_j}{\Delta x} \right)^2, \quad
E_B = \frac{EI_{lin}}{2} \Delta x \sum\nolimits'_J \chi_j^2
$$

and the works are increased at each step by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta W_F &= \Delta x \sum_I \bar{F}_i \delta y_i, \quad
\delta W_c = \frac{c}{\Delta t} \Delta x \sum_I \delta y_i^2, \quad
\delta W_\eta = (EI_{max} - EI_{min}) \chi_0 \Delta x \sum\nolimits'_J \bar{\eta}_j \delta \chi_j \\
\delta W_\chi &= \Delta x \sum\nolimits'_J \bar{M}_j \left( (D_2 \delta y)_j - \delta \chi_j \right) \\
\delta W_b &= \Delta x \sum\nolimits'_J \bar{M}_j (D_2 \delta y)_j - \Delta x \sum_I (D_2 \bar{M})_i \delta y_i
+ H \Delta x \sum_I (D_2 \bar{y})_i \delta y_i + \delta E_H
\end{aligned}
$$

$\bar{M} \delta \chi$ is exactly $\delta (EI_{lin} \chi^2 / 2)$ plus the
Bouc-Wen term, and $\delta W_b$ collects what summation by parts leaves at the
ends. These works take the forces at the middle of the step, which is what a
Crank-Nicolson step does. The generalized-$\alpha$ step differs in three
ways: its inertia term, weighted by $1 - \alpha_m$ and $\alpha_m$, is not the
increment of $E_k$, it weights the forces at $n+1$ and $n$ by $1 - \alpha_f$
and $\alpha_f$ instead of $1/2$, and its damping force uses
$(1 - \alpha_f) v^{n+1} + \alpha_f v^n$ instead of $\delta y / \Delta t$. The
work of these differences is

$$
\delta W_{num} = m \Delta x \sum_I \left( (1 - \alpha_m) a_i^{n+1} + \alpha_m a_i^n \right) \delta y_i - \delta E_k
+ \Delta x \sum_I \left( (\tfrac{1}{2} - \alpha_f) \left( (D_2 \delta M)_i - H (D_2 \delta y)_i - \delta F_i \right)
+ c \left( (1 - \alpha_f) v_i^{n+1} + \alpha_f v_i^n - \frac{\delta y_i}{\Delta t} \right) \right) \delta y_i
$$

zero up to the step residual for $\alpha_m = \alpha_f = 0$, where it is half the
difference of the equations at $n+1$ and $n$ times $\delta y$. The balance
therefore holds to the residual of each step: to round-off
for the constant model with the approximate curvature, to the Newton
tolerance otherwise.

Fixed supports are inert in the discrete balance too. On a 440 m span
($H$ = 31000 N, initial shape $0.5 \sin^3(\pi x / L)$ m, 400 steps per
period, 4 periods, constant model, approximate curvature), the drift of the
balance, ``numerical_work`` included, relative to the initial energy is:

| supports | ns | without ``boundary_work`` | with ``boundary_work`` |
|----------|----|---------------------------|------------------------|
| clamped | 201 | 1.4e-13 | 1.4e-13 |
| clamped | 401 | 4.1e-13 | 4.1e-13 |
| clamped | 801 | 3.9e-12 | 3.9e-12 |
| hinged | 201 | 1.5e-13 | 1.5e-13 |
| hinged | 401 | 4.2e-13 | 4.2e-13 |
| hinged | 801 | 3.4e-12 | 3.4e-12 |

``boundary_work`` is round-off at fixed clamped and hinged supports alike:
summation by parts of the solved rows leaves no term at the ends, the ghost
node moving with the first inner node (alike at a clamped end, opposite at a
hinged one) and the supports weighing 1/2 in the sums over $J$. The former
boundary rows, one-sided and without ghost nodes, left a work falling as
$\Delta x^3$ at hinged supports (3.9e-05 of the initial energy at
``ns = 201``). With moving supports (``dynamic_values``) ``boundary_work``
holds their physical work. The remaining drift is
the round-off of the $D_4$ operator, which grows like $EI / \Delta x^4$.

Limits:

* $E_k$ is summed on $I$: it leaves out the supports, whose velocity is set by
  the boundary rows, which is exact at fixed supports;
* on a Bouc-Wen step solved by the fallback (branch lagged, see
  [](`~slenderpy.beam.dynamic.solve_dynamic`)) the balance only holds to first
  order;
* the force is evaluated at the state of the previous step, as in the solver,
  so a state-dependent force is lagged by one step in ``external_work`` too;
* the coupled Stockbridge solver does not compute the balance.

### Compute cost

The works are accumulated at every time step, since they depend on the whole
path; the energies, functions of the state, are only computed at the output
steps. The balance thus adds a fixed number of vector operations on the
``ns`` nodes per step, about 55 $\mu$s at ``ns = 401``. Measured on the
440 m span with hinged supports, ``ns = 401``, 1600 steps with one output
every 10, gravity and a point excitation (fastest of 15 runs,
``compute_time``):

| case | ``energy=False`` | ``energy=True`` | overhead |
|------|------------------|-----------------|----------|
| constant model, approximate curvature | 0.106 s | 0.193 s | about 80 % |
| varying model, exact curvature | 0.70 s | 0.79 s | about 10 % |

The overhead shows in the linear case, where a step is a single triangular
solve (about 65 $\mu$s); it is small next to the Newton iterations of the
other cases (about 0.45 ms per step). The varying-model times spread by up to
25 % from one series of runs to the next, the overhead staying about 55 $\mu$s
per step.


## Boundary Conditions

For all the previous resolutions, there are always four boundary conditions. Two for each side of the beam:
the beam solvers raise a `ValueError` for a [](`~slenderpy.boundary_condition.BoundaryCondition`) of order 2.
Considering the left side of the beam at $x=0$ and the right side at $x=L$, the boundary conditions supported are under the form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 y(0,t) + b_1 \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(0,t) + c_1 \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}(0,t) = d_1(t) \\
a_2 y(0,t) + b_2 \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(0,t) + c_2 \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}(0,t) = d_2(t) \\
a_3 y(L,t) + b_3 \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(L,t) + c_3 \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}(L,t) = d_3(t) \\
a_4 y(L,t) + b_4 \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(L,t) + c_4 \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}(L,t) = d_4(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

Where $a_i, b_i, c_i \in \mathbb{R} \forall i \in \left\{1,2,3,4\right\}$ and $d_i(t) \forall i \in \left\{1,2,3,4\right\}$ can be function of time for the dynamic case and simply constant in the static case.
We denote by $y_0$ the displacement at $x=0$ and by $y_N$ the displacement at $x=L$, the span nodes $y_0, \dots, y_N$
being spaced by $\Delta x$. The relations are taken at the supports with the centered stencils, through a ghost node one
step beyond each support, $y_{-1}$ and $y_{N+1}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1 y_0 + b_1 \frac{y_1 - y_{-1}}{2 \Delta x} + c_1 \frac{y_{-1} - 2y_0 + y_1}{\Delta x^2} = d_1 \\
a_2 y_0 + b_2 \frac{y_1 - y_{-1}}{2 \Delta x} + c_2 \frac{y_{-1} - 2y_0 + y_1}{\Delta x^2} = d_2 \\
a_3 y_N + b_3 \frac{y_{N+1} - y_{N-1}}{2 \Delta x} + c_3 \frac{y_{N-1} - 2y_N + y_{N+1}}{\Delta x^2} = d_3 \\
a_4 y_N + b_4 \frac{y_{N+1} - y_{N-1}}{2 \Delta x} + c_4 \frac{y_{N-1} - 2y_N + y_{N+1}}{\Delta x^2} = d_4
\end{aligned}
$$

The beam equation is then solved at every span node between the supports, $y_1$ to $y_{N-1}$, its fourth difference at
$y_1$ and $y_{N-1}$ reaching the ghost nodes. These stencils are second order, and at fixed clamped or hinged supports
they keep the discrete energy exact: the ghost node moves with the first inner node, alike at a clamped end and opposite
at a hinged one, so the supports do no work (see [Energy balance](#energy-balance)). The former boundary rows, one-sided
at the supports without ghost nodes, imposed the slope with $(y_1 - y_0) / \Delta x$: first order, with an error that
spreads to the whole span, 75 mm of the 9.5 m sag of the 440 m span at 1 m cells against 1.9 mm now (see
[Space convergence](#space-convergence)).

The unknowns are the $N + 3$ values $y_{-1}, \dots, y_{N+1}$, and the four relations fill the two first and the two last
rows of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= \begin{pmatrix}
\frac{c_1}{\Delta x^2} - \frac{b_1}{2 \Delta x} & a_1 - \frac{2c_1}{\Delta x^2} & \frac{c_1}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{b_1}{2 \Delta x} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
\frac{c_2}{\Delta x^2} - \frac{b_2}{2 \Delta x} & a_2 - \frac{2c_2}{\Delta x^2} & \frac{c_2}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{b_2}{2 \Delta x} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & \frac{c_3}{\Delta x^2} - \frac{b_3}{2 \Delta x} & a_3 - \frac{2c_3}{\Delta x^2} & \frac{c_3}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{b_3}{2 \Delta x} \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & \frac{c_4}{\Delta x^2} - \frac{b_4}{2 \Delta x} & a_4 - \frac{2c_4}{\Delta x^2} & \frac{c_4}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{b_4}{2 \Delta x}
\end{pmatrix} \\
b &= \begin{pmatrix}
d_1\\
d_2\\
0 \\
\vdots \\
0 \\
d_3 \\
d_4
\end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix and vector the equation above are used for the static resolution. For the dynamic resolution the first linear system to solve in on the velocity,
we thus derivate with respect to time the equation above obtaining the same matrix $A$ than the equation above, since $\frac{\partial y}{\partial t} = v$,  and the vector $b$ contains the time derivative of
$d_i(t) \forall i \in \left\{1,2,3,4\right\}$.

Thus when using [](`~slenderpy.beam.dynamic.solve_dynamic`) the user should set `dynamic_values` with $\frac{\partial d_i}{\partial t} \forall i \in \left\{1,2,3,4\right\}$
in the [](`~slenderpy.boundary_condition.BoundaryCondition`) constructor. Each item is a callable `f(x, t)`, evaluated at the
bound its condition applies to ($x = 0$ for $d_1, d_2$, $x = L$ for $d_3, d_4$), and the tuple follows the rows from the
first to the last node: $(d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4)$ is `(left[0], left[1], right[1], right[0])`.

The ghost nodes of the initial state follow from the relations
([](`~slenderpy.boundary_condition.BoundaryCondition.extend`)): at each end, the relation that involves the ghost node, the
slope of a clamped end or the curvature of a hinged one, sets it, with the constant $d_i$ for the position and the values
of `dynamic_values` at `t0` for the velocity (zero without them). The constant $d_i$ are thus the boundary values at `t0`.
The other relation of each end, such as $y_0 = d_1$, is read from the initial position, and without `dynamic_values` the
dynamic solve keeps the boundary values of the initial state.
